text: Part five is the only part of the whole plan that stops and asks me before it builds anything. I want to explain why that is, because deciding where to put a checkpoint is a real skill and this is the clearest example of it all week.
Everything before this was reversible. If part three had come out wrong I would have thrown it away and asked again, and lost twenty minutes.
The database is different, and not because it is hard. Because everything after it is shaped by it.
Parts six, seven, eight, nine and ten all assume the shape we agree on right now. Get it wrong and you do not lose part five. You lose everything built on top of it.
So the rule for where the checkpoints go is not how difficult is this. It is how much of what comes next depends on it.
And that is a question you can answer without knowing anything about databases, which is rather the point.
Now, what it actually came back with, and I am going to translate the whole thing because none of it needs jargon.
A table is a spreadsheet. Rows are records, columns are fields. That is genuinely the whole idea, and everything else is bookkeeping about how the spreadsheets refer to each other.
It designed four of them. Users. Boards. Columns. Cards.
Users is one row per person. For us that is one row, because the whole app has one login. But the table is built as though there could be thousands, which is deliberate.
Boards is one row per board, and each row carries the identifier of the user it belongs to. That single number is the whole relationship. Board seven belongs to user three.
Columns is one row per column, each pointing at its board, each with a name and a position. Position is just a number saying which comes first.
And cards is one row per card, pointing at its board and its column, with a title, a description, and a position of its own.
And now the sentence that makes the whole design make sense. Moving a card between columns is changing one number in one row.
That is it. Change which column the card points at, tidy up the positions, done. All that dragging on screen, and underneath it is one field changing value.
Now the part I want to be honest about, because it is the counterweight to everything I have said this week about staying in the loop.
I had a design in my head before I asked. I was going to store the entire board as one blob of text against the user. One row. The whole thing in it.
And that would have worked, for this. It is also the hacky answer, and I know it is the hacky answer, and I would have done it anyway because it is quick.
Its version is better than mine. Not slightly. Properly better, and in a way I can explain to you, which is the test of whether I actually understand why.
With my blob, finding all the cards in one column means reading the whole board out and picking through it. With its version, that is a question you can just ask.
And with my blob, adding a second board or a second user later means unpicking the format and rewriting everything that touches it. With its version, it is another row.
So I approved its design over my own. And I want you to sit with the fact that this is the same lecture where I will spend five minutes telling you it got stuck in a loop for half an hour.
Both of those are true at once. It is better than me at some things and worse at others, and the whole skill is knowing which is which today.
I did not approve it silently, though, and this is the bit I would encourage you to copy even when you are not sure.
One thing in there looked awkward to me. It had put a rule on the columns saying no two of them may sit in the same position.
Which sounds obviously correct, and might not be. Because when you reorder a list, there is usually a moment in the middle where two things briefly occupy the same slot before everything settles.
I do not know whether that is a problem here. I genuinely do not. So I did not tell it to change it.
I described the concern, asked whether it causes the thing I am worried about, and said if it does, change it, and if it does not, leave it alone.
That shape is worth memorising. Here is what worries me, here is why, you decide. It gets you the benefit of the doubt without pretending to expertise you do not have.
And it costs nothing. If I am wrong, I have lost one sentence and learned something. If I am right, I have caught a design flaw before a single row existed.
And here is what came back, which is better than I expected and slightly better than I deserved.
Yes. The reorder would have collided. Two cards would have briefly claimed the same position during a move between columns, and the database would have refused the whole thing.
But it did not remove the rule, which is what I would have done. It kept the rule and changed how a move works, so the positions are tidied on the way through and the collision never occurs.
So the guarantee survives and the problem goes away. That is a genuinely better answer than either of the two I had in my head.

And look at what it cost me. I did not know whether there was a problem. I could not have told you what the fix would be. All I had was a feeling that one rule looked uncomfortable, and I said so out loud.
That is the entire skill. Not expertise. Noticing the thing that makes you uneasy and refusing to let it past without a sentence.
One more thing before we move on. It finished part five, and then it stopped, and asked whether I wanted it to carry on.
It did that because the plan told it to, four hours ago, in writing. And it remembered.
Which is the return on having written the plan at all. The stop is not something I have to remember to enforce in the moment. It is built into the thing being followed.
Part six is the back end routes, and it is the shortest explanation of the day.
A route is a question the back end knows how to answer. What is on my board. Move this card to that column. Rename this column.
Each one is an address plus a rule. Something asks at that address, the back end does the work, and answers.
And that is genuinely all a back end is. A list of questions it knows how to answer, and the code that answers them.
At the end of part six they all exist and nothing on screen has changed at all, because nobody is asking them yet.
Which is worth pausing on, because it is the first time today that finishing a part produced no visible difference whatsoever.
If you were judging progress by the screen you would think it had done nothing. The screen is not the measure. That is what the checklist in the plan is for.
Part seven is the one that joins the two halves, and it is the most significant change in the whole build.
Up to now the board has been drawing itself. The cards you have been looking at are written into the front end, the same five columns every time you reload, because nothing was ever saved.
After part seven, the board asks the back end what is on it, and tells the back end when anything moves.
Which is the difference between a picture of an application and an application.
And it is the biggest change so far by a wide margin, so I expect it to take a while and I expect it to be messy.
